en: *Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Dhāraṇī*, one fascicle.
Compiled by Kai-fu-yi-tong-san-si Te-jin Shi Hong-lu-qing Su-guo-gong, who held an estate of three thousand households,
was granted purple robes, and was posthumously honored with the title of Si-tong-san-si.
Regarding Vajrapāṇi, the *Yogatantra-ṭīkā* states: Translated by the śramaṇa Amoghavajra, Tripitaka Master of Daguangzhi Daxingshan Temple, posthumously titled Dajian, by imperial decree.
As for Vajrapāṇi, the *Yogatantra-ṭīkā* says:
Holding a vajra in his hand symbolizes that internally he possesses great bodhicitta,
while externally he subdues all afflictions.
Therefore he is named Vajrapāṇi.
Another explanation states that he cannot be destroyed by the three kinds of Māras.
The essence of bodhicitta is firm and solid, becoming vajra-wisdom;
it is established by all Tathāgatas and is capable of shattering the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism.
Therefore, because he shatters the mountain of false views with the vajra-wisdom mallet and realizes the adamantine concentration (vajrasamādhi) which he constantly holds in the palm of his hand,
he is named Vajrapāṇi.
What is the meaning of "bodhisattva"?
It is one who awakens to the true Dharma;
having awakened, they abide within saṃsāra.
Because he causes all sentient beings to awaken,
he is called a bodhisattva. Furthermore,
it is said that "bodhi" carries the meaning of "to awaken."
*Sattva* means a sentient being;
it is also called "mind" and "valiant.
*Mahā* means "great."
"Sattva" means courageous and valiant; it refers to one who is not timid or weak,
having accumulated the two kinds of provisions throughout three great incalculable eons.
Therefore, he is called a Mahāsattva.
What is meant by "Vajramaṇi"? (In Chinese, this is translated as) "this jewel.
"Vajra" is explained as before.
There are six meanings of "jewel" (ratna):
first, because it is difficult to obtain;
second, because it is pure and free from defilement.
Third, because they possess great majestic power;
fourth, because they adorn the world;
fifth, because they are exceptionally superior and peerless.
Sixth, because it is unchanging.
First, regarding "difficult to encounter":
it is extremely difficult to meet with the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.
Second, "pure and stainless" refers to the purity and stainlessness attained through practicing according to the teachings and realizing bodhi.
Third, "of great majestic power" refers to...
Because one who possesses the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and exercises mastery over transformations is called "of Great Majestic Virtue" (*mahātejas*).
Regarding "adorned with the four [kinds of] adornments for the world":
by means of the three types of bodhisattva ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because it adorns the body and mind;
fifth, because its excellence is peerless,
for having realized unsurpassed bodhi, it is uniquely honored and peerlessly supreme within the three realms.
The six are unchanging because they have realized the ultimate, unsurpassed bodhi which is immutable;
thus, they are like a vajra-maṇi.
He is known by the name Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva.
For this reason, this bodhisattva holds a vajra-jewel in his hand;
"vajra" signifies sharpness.
The Prajñāpāramitā is a vajra-sharp sword that can sever the seeds of affliction;
it is the all-encompassing vajra-sharpness.
He is known by the name Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva;
for this reason, this bodhisattva holds a vajra-sword in his hand.
As for the Vajrayakṣa Bodhisattva:
The meaning of *vajra* is as explained previously.
*Yakṣa* means "fierce" and is also said to mean "exhaustive.
It is the fifteenth wisdom within the sixteen wisdoms of Samantabhadra’s practice.
It is named the Wisdom of the Exhaustion of All Things as Vajra; by means of the wisdom-fang of the Vajra Yakṣa,
it devours all afflictions and secondary afflictions.
Exhausted without remainder.
The vajra bell symbolizes the meaning of Prajñāpāramitā.
Shaking the bell to awaken the ignorant and ordinary beings:
upon hearing the sound of the bell once,
they realize the Prajñāpāramitā.
He is named the Bodhisattva Destroyer of All Māra-Enemies;
for this reason, this Bodhisattva holds a vajra-bell in his hand.
As for the Bodhisattva Vajrapāramitā:
The meaning of "Vajra" is as explained previously.
The meaning of "Pāramitā" as "reaching the other shore" is as explained by the former masters.
Now, following the treatises on grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), I shall analyze the sentence by its components: *pāramitā*.
*Pāra* has the meaning of "the other shore."
The term "I-shang-duo" (Ita-udra) carries the meaning of "this shore.
Because this Bodhisattva holds the vajra-wheel,
after Vairocana Buddha has attained enlightenment in the upper realm, [the Bodhisattva]...
This Bodhisattva requests the Tathāgata to turn the Dharma wheel of the Vajrayāna.
By means of this Dharma wheel, which is a boat of Prajñā,
he shall ferry immeasurable and boundless sentient beings from this shore.
Having reached the shore of non-abiding nirvāṇa,
he is known by the manifest name Bodhisattva Who Turns the Wheel of Dharma upon the Mere Arising of the Thought of Enlightenment. *Namo ratnatrayāya*.
*Tāraye*. This is the meaning of taking refuge in the Triple Gem.
If there is a person who upholds this sutra...
By taking refuge in the Jewel of the Buddha,
one immediately obtains the five families of Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattvas,
who attend and protect one with immeasurable retinues.
He empowers that person.
This bodhicitta of the Bodhisattva is noble,
for the Buddha is born from bodhicitta.
By taking refuge in the Dharma Jewel, one obtains the protection of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with his retinue and the Four Great Kings. Why is this?
Because when Śakra is in peril, [he turns to the Dharma].
Through the empowerment of Prajñā, one obtains benefit in this very life;
therefore, Śakra, Lord of Devas, honors the Jewel of the Dharma and takes refuge in the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Then the King of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, together with the gods of the Five Pure Abodes and their retinues,
will provide protection and support for the upholder of this sutra,
[establishing him] within the Five Pure Abodes.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas and the assembly of Śrāvakas constantly dwell in that heaven,
abiding in the joy of the Dharma in the present life;
they are all held in high esteem by the Brahmās and others.
*Namo āryāvalokiteśvarāya tathāgatāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya.* *Namaḥ* has the meaning of "taking refuge."
It is also called "bowing one's head" (*kṣipta-śiras*) and "prostrating with the crown of the head" (*praṇāma*).
*Arya* has the meaning of "one who wards off evil" (*ari-ghna*);
the interpretation in this region explains it as "the Noble One" (*ārya*).
*Vairocana* means "all-illuminating"; it is also called Mahāvairocana.
Its meaning is like that of the sun in the world.
It illuminates one side but not the other; it illuminates the day but not the night;
it illuminates one world but not other worlds.
It may be called "the sun," but it cannot be called "Mahāvairocana."
Vairocana, the Great Sun, is both the form body and the dharma body,
pervading the entire dharma realm and the realm of space throughout the boundless worlds of the ten directions.
They shine universally upon all.
If a person knows these merits and benefits of the Buddha,
they should take refuge in him and pay him homage.

Then one shall obtain the empowerment, protection, and mindfulness of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the eight classes of holy beings throughout the entirety of empty space and the pervasive Dharma-realm. *Tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya.*
The meaning of "Tathāgata, Arhat,
Samyaksaṃbuddha" has already been explained previously. *Namo 'ryāya*.
This has already been explained. Regarding *samantabhadra*:
*samanta* means "universal" (*pūrvārtha*).
*Vajra* means "noble" (*bhadra*).
The letter *ya* refers to "sound" (*śabda*) within the seven cases (*vibhakti*) of the eightfold declension (*aṣṭavibhakti*) according to the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*);
the same applies below.
This Bodhisattva expounds the gate of the three mysteries and the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
If all Buddhas do not cultivate the gate of the three mysteries,
they do not practice the conduct of Samantabhadra.
It is impossible for one to attain Buddhahood;
and once Buddhahood has been attained, it is likewise impossible for one to cease the practices of Samantabhadra through the three secret gates.
To Bodhisattva; to Mahāsattva.
The meaning of Mahāsattva:
*mahākāruṇika* means "one of great compassion."
If one takes refuge in the noble Bodhisattva Samantabhadra,
then all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions will provide their protection;
[so shall] all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
All have attained realization of the sacred fruit by practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra through the gateway of the three mysteries;
for this reason, they are noble and venerable.
*Tadyathā*. "Thus it was said.
The above is the homage to the Triple Gem, Vairocana Buddha, and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
*Ki-raṅ-na pra-ṇi-bhe*: the explicit meaning of the phrase is explained as the lamp of wisdom;
the esoteric meaning of the phrase is explained as taking non-apprehension as the skillful means.
Non-intelligence and non-attainment constitute the lamp of wisdom of the *prajñāpāramitā*,
which is able to illumine all Buddha-dharmas.
The character "evil" (*è*)— this character "evil" is actually the character "a" (*ǎ*) in the Sanskrit original.
For the sake of following the convenience of the words and phrases,
it is pronounced as "kṣayāśe."
This reveals and explains the meaning of the inexhaustible treasury.
In the cryptic phrase, the single syllable *a* is explained as the seed-syllable.
The syllable *a* signifies that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.
The syllable A is the mother of all syllables;
it can give birth to all phenomena.
If one can understand the gateway of the syllable A, [one understands all things].
Through union with yoga,
one attains the inexhaustible treasury of the Buddha-dharma and realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.
Just as space is of a single characteristic, pure, and equal,
it becomes non-conceptual wisdom (*avikalpa-jñāna*). *Pratibhānavati*.
The commentary on the manifest phrases possesses eloquence;
in the commentary on the secret phrases, within this very phrase,
one takes the two syllables *pra* and *ra* and merges them into a single syllable.
It serves as the seed.
The syllable *pra* represents the non-apprehension of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
thus, one takes non-apprehension as the skillful means.

Within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), because one realizes that all phenomena arise through causes and conditions and because one realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen,
one attains the inexhaustible treasury of the Buddha-dharma.
In the subsequently attained wisdom, one attains the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) and mastery in preaching the Dharma. *Sarvabuddhāvalokite*.
The "Manifested Syllables" (vyañjana-pada) explain the meaning observed by all Buddhas.
The "Secret Syllables" (guhya-pada) explain that the single syllable *sa* serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The syllable *sa* signifies the equality of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-samatā*).
Because the subject that perceives and the object perceived are equal and identical,
and because neither the grasper nor the grasped can be apprehended,
one realizes suchness.
May the infinite Buddhas of the stream of Dharma observe and protect me.
This is the *Gaṇapatinirghaṇṭa*, a commentary on the words that reveals the meaning of the perfected yoga (*yoganiṣpanna*).
In the commentary on the secret mantra, the single syllable *yu* is taken as the seed-syllable.
The syllable *yu* signifies that there is nothing to be apprehended in any vehicle (*yāna*).
If one is in union with the wisdom of yogic contemplation, [this is realized].
Having realized perfect completion,
one fully realizes the single true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) within the teachings, principles, practices, and fruits of all vehicles.
*Yan-bi-’in-ra-nu-ra-va-ga-ṅe*:
This explanatory phrase clarifies the profound and unfathomable meaning;
this cryptic phrase explains that the single syllable *yan* serves as the seed-syllable.
The character "Yan" (Dignified) signifies that all *tathatā* (suchness) phenomena neither come nor go, just as one realizes the ocean of *tathatā*.
The *prajñā* of the true mark cannot be expressed through words;
it is the realm of the Buddhas, realized through the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
*Tirya-tva-pariniṣpanna*: This is the explanatory phrase (*vyākhyā*) for the meaning of the "manifest word" (*vyañjana-pada*), which signifies the perfect accomplishment of the three times. *Tirya*:
This is the explanatory phrase for the "secret word" (*mantra-pada*); the Sanskrit syllable *tri* is a single syllable, and this single syllable serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
*Ṭirya* means that all phenomena are the accomplishment of the self-nature of the equality of *tathatā*,
surpassing the number of grains of sand in the Ganges River within the *tathatā* of merit.

There are no past, future, or present false discriminations, nor any formations dissociated from mind, nor any stubborn attachment or delusion regarding conditioned phenomena. *Bhūmi-jñāna-sañjñā-nī*.
The "Exposition of Manifest Words" explains the meaning of generating the bodhicitta;
the "Exposition of Secret Words" explains that the single syllable *mau* serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The syllable *mau* signifies that all phenomena are without bondage.
If one knows that the bodhicitta within one's own body is spontaneously accomplished as equal throughout the three periods of time,
like space, free from all manifold phenomena.
Thus, knowing that the minds of all sentient beings and the minds of all Buddhas are as pure as one's own mind,
one gives rise to great compassion and feels profound pity.
Then, by employing various skillful means,
one causes all sentient beings to reach the ultimate state,
where they are free from suffering, liberated, and neither bound nor unbound.
*Sarvavisakavisekṛti*: The manifest phrase explains the meaning of obtaining the crown-consecration (mūrdhābhiṣeka) through all sprinklings;
the secret phrase explains that the single syllable *sa* serves as the seed-syllable.
The syllable *sa* signifies that all phenomena are without defilement and without attachment.
This is because one observes that the minds of oneself, others, and all Buddhas are identical in their single suchness,
which is the great compassion of the same essence.
Therefore, being unstained and unattached,
one receives the consecration of the water of all Tathāgata-dharmas within emptiness,
thereby attaining the empowerment of the three karmas.
He possesses mastery in teaching the Dharma within the immeasurable collection of sūtras;
he is Dharmasāgara-sambuddhi.
The "Exposition of Manifested Phrases" explains the meaning of the arising of the ocean of Dharma;
the "Exposition of Secret Phrases" explains that the single syllable *da* is the seed-syllable.
The syllable *da* signifies the meaning of non-apprehension within the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
By abiding in a mind of non-apprehension,
the innate grasping at a self within the ālayavijñāna and the seeds of innate grasping at phenomena [are eliminated].
By means of the great sage Mañjuśrī’s adamantine sharp sword,
one eternally severs all meanings without remainder;
thus, the teachings that are the outflow of the pure dharmadhātu emerge.
This constitutes the meaning of the arising of the ocean of dharmas.
The syllable *da* is the seed-syllable of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. *Amoghaśravaṇe*.
The *Vyākhyāyukti* explains the term *amogha*;
whereas ancient commentators explained it as "not empty," I shall now explain it according to the treatises on grammatical science (*śabdavidyā*).
Regarding the meaning of "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*): the single syllable *A* serves as the seed-syllable.
As for the syllable *A*, all phenomena are from the very beginning quiescent and from the very beginning in nirvāṇa.
By realizing this seal of the dharma of liberation,
one hears the teachings heard before the Buddhas within the great assemblies throughout the entire dharma-realm and all buddha-fields.
"May all be maintained and never forgotten! Mahā-samanta-vardhana-bhūmi-nirdeśa-tīkā.
This title reveals and explains the meaning of the Great Stage of Samantabhadra.
In the commentary on the secret mantra, the single syllable *ma* serves as the seed-syllable.
The syllable *ma* signifies the meaning of "selflessness" (*anātman*) regarding all phenomena.
There are two kinds of selflessness.
There is the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena.
If a practitioner of yoga realizes these two forms of selflessness,
they emerge from the stage of Great Samantabhadra.
Realizing the perfectly pure Dharma-body of Vairocana, adorned with a hundred merits: *Vijrakaraṇapari-prāpnoti*.
The *Vyakhyāpada* explains the meaning of obtaining a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*).
The ancient text explains the meaning of bestowing a prophecy.
The *Guhyapada* explains that the two syllables *vi* and *ya* combined as one constitute the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The syllable *va* signifies that all phenomena are pervasive and ungraspable; it means that one knows all phenomena to be quiescent in their intrinsic nature and nirvana by intrinsic nature.
Both the subject that realizes and the object realized are of one and the same nature.
"Neither increasing nor decreasing, perfectly realizing the Dharma-realm:
*sarvasiddhānāṃ namaḥ siddhe*. This phrase elucidates the meaning of "homage to all those who have attained accomplishment."
The "Accomplisher" (*siddha*) is an alternative name for a bodhisattva.
In the explanation of the secret mantra, the single syllable *sa* is taken as the seed-syllable.
The syllable *sa* signifies that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) lack solidity.
In every thought-moment, the four characteristics undergo transition, flow, cessation, and destruction.
Within the syllable *sa* is the syllable *a*. If one realizes the gateway of the syllable *a*, [one realizes the non-arising of all phenomena].
Originally unborn and undying, it is also eternal, constant, and firm;
like a vajra, the mind attains mastery and can manifest various bodies.
*Sarvabodhisattvasañjanani*: In its exoteric interpretation, this reveals the meaning of the arising of all bodhisattvas;
in its esoteric interpretation, it takes the single syllable *sa* as the seed-syllable.
The syllable *sa* signifies the meaning of the equality of all phenomena.
By contemplating this syllable,
the mind becomes equal and perfectly equal with *prajñā*.
The single characteristic of purity throughout preceding and succeeding moments,
which is able to give rise to all pāramitās and all stages,
is precisely named Prajñāpāramitā, the Mother of Buddhas.
*Bhagavatī buddhamātā* means "the Blessed Mother of the Buddhas";
*bhagavat* is used here in the masculine gender.
*Bhagavatī* is the feminine form; when both [the masculine and feminine] are combined according to their intended meaning, it is explained as having the sense of "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*).
However, according to the etymological analysis of grammatical treatises (*śabda-vidyā*), this is not the case when confronting an opponent.
*Bhaga* means "to destroy," and *van* means "able.
One who is able to destroy the four māras is called Bhagavān.

Furthermore, another interpretation explains *phala* (薄阿梵) by analyzing its syllables according to the science of phonology (*śabda-śāstra*). The syllable *pha* is interpreted as "to break" (*bhañjana*), while *ala* signifies "thorough knowledge" (*parijñāna*).
Thus, it means "the thorough knowledge that breaks [defilements]."
The letter A is said to mean "not existent" and also "not non-existent.

It is because the Buddha has realized that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, neither identical nor different, neither eternal nor annihilated, and neither increasing nor decreasing.
Because the Buddha possesses such merits, he is named Bhagavat.
Another explanation states that Bhagavat is one who is fully endowed with the two kinds of provisions: merit and wisdom.
Regarding the two kinds of provisions (*sambhāra*):
*bhagavatī* has the meaning of the feminine suffix;
the explanation is as before.
In the commentary on the secret mantra, the single syllable *bha* serves as the seed-syllable. Regarding the syllable *bha*:
all phenomena (*dharmas*) have no existence that can be apprehended. "Existence" here carries the meaning of the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*).
Therefore, the three realms are mind-only.
By the defilement of the mind, sentient beings are defiled;
by the purification of the mind, sentient beings are purified.
If one follows the teachings of the Exoteric Vehicle,
the practice of contemplative prajñā acts as the generative cause, manifesting the capacity to give birth to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
For this reason, she is called the Mother of the Buddhas.
This has been explained from the beginning up until the phrase "Mother of the Buddhas."
Within the Yoga teachings,
the sixteen practices of Samantabhadra’s conduct are established,
just as there are sixteen aspects within the path of seeing (darśanamārga) of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
*Arane kāre aruṇakāre*. The syllable *A* is the gateway to the fact that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen;
by knowing that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, one enters the state of all phenomena being free from dust.
Therefore, the syllable-ra gate signifies that all phenomena are free from dust;
by knowing that all phenomena are free from dust,
one enters the non-contention of all phenomena.
Therefore, the letter-door *nai* signifies that all dharmas are without contention;
because one knows that all dharmas are without contention,
one immediately enters into the non-activity of all dharmas.
Therefore, the gateway of the letter Ka signifies that all phenomena are without fabrication;
by knowing that all phenomena are without fabrication,
one enters the purity of all phenomena.
Therefore, the letter-gateway *ra* signifies that all phenomena (*dharma*) are pure.
Because one knows that all phenomena are pure,
one enters into the non-contention (*araṇa*) of all phenomena.
Therefore, the syllable *nai* is the gateway to the fact that all phenomena are without contention;
because one knows that all phenomena are without contention,
one enters into the primordial tranquility of all phenomena.
Therefore, the gateway of the letter A is that all phenomena are primordially quiescent.
By knowing that all phenomena are primordially quiescent,
one enters into the stainlessness of all phenomena.
Therefore, the letter-gateway *ra* signifies that all phenomena are stainless.
By knowing that all phenomena are stainless,
one enters into the non-contention of all phenomena.
Therefore, by means of the gateway of the syllable *ṇa*, all phenomena are without contention;
because one knows that all phenomena are without contention,
one immediately enters into the non-activity of all phenomena.
Therefore, the letter-gate *ka* signifies that all phenomena are without fabrication;
by knowing that all phenomena are without fabrication,
one enters non-conceptual wisdom.
Therefore, the letter-gateway *ra* signifies that all phenomena are without conceptual differentiation.
By knowing that all phenomena are without conceptual differentiation,
one immediately enters the immovability of all phenomena.
Therefore, the letter-gateway *nai* signifies that all phenomena are immovable.
By knowing that all phenomena are immovable,
one realizes the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā*: This reveals the meaning of the phrase "Great Wisdom Reaching the Other Shore," because one realizes the Great Prajñāpāramitā.
That is to say, based on non-abiding nirvāṇa.
The phrase *svāhā* explains non-abiding nirvāṇa;
thus, it is based on non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Until the end of the future limit,
may they extensively bring benefit and happiness to boundless sentient beings.
*Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Dhāraṇī*, one fascicle.
